summary: Solicits white papers on topics related to the requirements and selection criteria for IPng, the next generation of IP. It is a call for input, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1550 invited interested people to write white papers about requirements for IPng, the next generation of IP. It explains how papers would be reviewed and published, and suggests engineering topics for authors to address.

subtitle: A call for papers about requirements and selection criteria for the next generation of IP.

tldr.problem: The IETF IPng area wanted input on requirements for a next-generation Internet Protocol and factors that should influence its selection.
tldr.mechanism: The memo invites white papers, sets a review and publication process, gives format limits, and lists engineering topics for authors to consider.
tldr.outcome: It is a historical call for input, not a protocol. Its submission deadline was February 1, 1994.

today: RFC 1550 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its submission deadline of February 1, 1994 has passed; the document is a call for input, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: The Call for White Papers
sections.content:
The IPng area in the IETF invited interested parties to submit white papers about requirements and selection criteria for IPng. Authors could describe a particular requirement or a factor that might affect the selection. The RFC gives future utility meters and wireless network links as examples of topics.

At the time of the call, papers evaluating specific IPng proposals were not accepted. The memo set February 1, 1994 as the submission deadline and gave an email address for papers and questions.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF asked people to explain what they needed from the next generation of IP. The call was for requirements and selection factors, not evaluations of specific proposals.

sections.title: Review and Publication
sections.content:
Submitted papers first receive a clarity review by members of the IPng directorate and external review board. A separate technical review assesses feasibility without making value judgments. Either review may produce suggestions for the author.

After review and any revisions chosen by the author, a paper is submitted as an Internet-Draft. After a suitable period, it is to be submitted as an Informational RFC unless the author withdraws it. The RFC says the papers would form part of the historical record of the IPng process.
sections.plainLanguage: Reviewers check whether a paper is clear and technically feasible. After that, it is submitted as an Internet-Draft and later as an Informational RFC unless the author withdraws it.

sections.title: Paper Format and Outline
sections.content:
Papers must follow the format requirements in RFC 1543 and must not exceed 10 pages. The reference version must be ASCII; an additional PostScript version may be submitted. The paper should start with an executive summary of no more than half a page and then address the issues the author considers important.

Authors could submit more than one paper. The RFC includes the relevant ASCII formatting rules in an appendix, including limits on lines per page and characters per line.
sections.plainLanguage: A paper could be no longer than 10 pages and had to include a short opening summary. The reference copy had to use ASCII, with PostScript allowed as an additional version.

sections.title: Suggested Engineering Topics
sections.content:
The memo lists 16 topics raised in earlier discussions, in no particular order. They include scaling, transition and deployment, security, mobile hosts, resource reservation, policy-based routing, datagram service, accounting, communication media, robustness, and suggested action items. Authors could address these or another relevant topic.

For scaling, the RFC states that common wisdom at the time was that IPng should handle 10 to the 12th nodes. It also says papers about timescale and transition would be forwarded to the relevant working groups.
sections.plainLanguage: The list helps authors consider areas such as network growth, security, mobility, and transition. It is a set of suggested topics, not a specification for IPng.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it raises no security issues. It invites comments on the security requirements that IPng should meet.
sections.plainLanguage: The solicitation does not define security features. It asks authors to discuss security requirements for IPng.

references.text: Postel, J. and J. Reynolds, Instructions to RFC Authors, RFC 1543, October 1993.
